Senses.Explanation: Rely on power to bully others describes using an advantageous position against someone else. Hongzhi immediately restates it as using strength against weakness; Tianyin applies it after a king imposes a severe condition; Nanyue contrasts it with departing without such conduct; and the source-identified fourth speaker says it makes people afraid.

Senses.Explanation: A long sword reaching the sky names an outsized sword image used through explicit comparisons and predicates. Wuyi Yuanlai says that ‘this one thought’ is like the sword (這一念子如倚天長劍): anything touching its edge cannot be got at all, while lingering and grinding it dull means the sword has long been gone. Yuanwu Keqin describes the sword with ‘stern, awe-inspiring power’ (凜凜神威) and pairs it with the clear radiance of the sun. Yulin Tongxiu raises his staff and answers, ‘the sky-reaching long sword chills the person before it’ (倚天長劍逼人寒). Lianfeng Su imagines a person holding it and cutting eighty-one fascicles of ‘tangled vines’ like one skein, ‘one cut, all severed’ (將八十一卷爛葛藤如斬一綟絲，一斬一切斷). In the sole retained lamp recension, Ganlu Deyong compares Deshan Xuanjian’s blow to the sword and Linji Yixuan’s phrase to thunder on dry ground, then calls both ‘relying on force and raising waves without wind’ (盡是倚勢欺人無風起浪). These passages establish the towering sword, its edge, its power, its cold, and its cutting; they do not assign every sword occurrence one further meaning.

Senses.Explanation: Before the Stupa of Many Sons — the spot the tradition fixes for the first handing-over, and the emblem Chan rows reach for whenever a robe moves, an heir is weighed, or the old news is raised once more. Yuanwu Keqin, opening the hall for the invited elder of Changlu: before the Stupa of Many Sons the half-seat was shared, the stream cut off; at Shaolin nine years seated still, a wall of ten-thousand fathoms — rousing the smith's bellows, applying the upward tongs, the great function and great machine wholly alive and wholly killing, drawing nails and stripping glue for everyone; and Mi'an Xianjie, at the sovereign's birthday: the forest-dweller — how shall he repay the grace? The news before the Stupa of Many Sons stands; each time it is raised, it is new. Hanyue Fazang, raising the robe his own teacher at Jinsu had sent: ever since before the Stupa of Many Sons it wrapped Kasyapa, he has sat cold to this day before Cockfoot Peak; in the room at Huangmei it fenced the Sixth Patriarch, and under the horse's hooves the bustle has not stopped — and today it is handed on down the generations to the hall of Quiet Rest, and on close inspection is only good for wrapping a thirty-year-old broken straw sandal; Yongjue Yuanxian, at a layman's robe-gift: before the Stupa of Many Sons, the pillars and the lanterns butt heads; at midnight in Huangmei, the black cat and the white calf cross in study — just at that moment, what was handed over? He lifts the corner of the kasaya: not woven by the Weaver Maid, but all the mother-of-change's loom; one thread running through, and it can shade heaven and cover earth; truly not an inch of silk hung, and then it may range seven ways and eight. Juelang Daosheng, sending the warden-layman into the room: the Tathagata of Jinsu once occupied this room, today the coast re-raises the line's wind — and closes: before the Stupa of Many Sons he knows my nobility; outside the night-lit curtain the king of the teaching is honored — take care! Baichi Xingyuan, at the hall held for the patron praying for an heir: the news before the Stupa of Many Sons stands; one raising, one renewal — then raises the old case, the monk asking Xinghua: before the Stupa of Many Sons, what was to be discussed? One man passes on emptiness, ten thousand pass it on as fact — the master stamps him: the ready sword of life-and-death, that old man of Xinghua; and Yuanjie Ying, at the decade-memorial handing the robe to the elder of the west hall: before the Stupa of Many Sons it was never finished; the handing-on has gone round until today — this mountain monk with both hands gives it over in person: five petals, one flower, spring across the great earth. And the scene that set the standard: Baiyu Jingsi's lineage-source cycle retells the fourteenth patriarch Tongan Guanzhi attending the earlier Tongan — Tongan Daopi at the point of death ascending the hall: before the Stupa of Many Sons the true heir shows; before Five Elders Peak, how stands the matter? Asked three times, none answered — then the master came out: outside the night-lit curtain, standing in rank; ten thousand miles of song proclaim the great peace. The dying one said: it had to be this blind fellow. Baiyu's own verse on it: the old man never resting his mind, alas — teaching his boy to busy himself keeping house.

Zhuanyu Guanheng explicitly quotes Laozi in a preface for a gifted young layman whose eloquence he respects. Naming him Ruone, 'as if inarticulate,' he explains that appearing inarticulate need not mean lacking understanding, and follows the headword with the warning that language leaks even when its meaning is rounded. He contrasts verbose loss of inward illumination with restraint that keeps it present. Yet he also forbids treating silence itself as marvelous: one should speak when speech is appropriate and be silent when silence is appropriate, remaining lively rather than stuck on one side. The quotation disciplines eloquence without condemning it absolutely.

Senses.Explanation: "Much speech is worse than little; little is worse than silence" ranks explanations down to none, then dares the speaker to respond anyway. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J28/J28nB213.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhiyan Xiu. Zhiyan Xiu quotes scripture saying that throughout the lands in all directions there is only one path of teaching, followed by the stronger claim that there are not even two, much less three. He then asks whether his former teacher's decades of preaching throughout Jiangnan and Zhejiang should be called that one path. Calling it one, he says, sends one to hell as swiftly as an arrow; refusing that name does the same. He asks whether anyone in the assembly can get out of this predicament. His ensuing praise of his lineage brother at Bao'an for carrying their teacher's work forward belongs to this setting of transmission. The quotation therefore tests how to speak of an actual teacher's many teachings without settling into either verbal alternative. The immediate source introduces it simply as scripture; it does not name an individual speaker for the quoted clause.

Miyin Zhenchuan first answers a monk asking about teaching that has no interruption: falling willow catkins give way to the cuckoo's cry. Further questions about sameness and flowing together lead him to say that understanding here reveals no interruption in the teaching. He explicitly attributes the quoted claim about there not being two paths, much less three, to the Buddha. Miyin then asks whether drums on the eastern mountain, bells at the western temple, a noisy front gate and a quiet rear hall are the one path of teaching. Denying it is like holding stolen goods while protesting innocence; affirming it may amount to calling a jar a bell. He urges a decisive cutting through of the hesitation and challenges anyone who can escape his mirror-like scrutiny to speak. The old clause remains the locally attributed Buddha's voice; Miyin supplies the present questions and challenge. The passage puts the claim to work amid contrasting sounds and places rather than merely listing doctrinal divisions.

Senses.Explanation: There are not even two paths of teaching, much less three. Zhiyan Xiu quotes scripture saying that throughout the lands in all directions there is only one path of teaching, followed by the stronger claim that there are not even two, much less three. He then asks whether his former teacher's decades of preaching throughout Jiangnan and Zhejiang should be called that one path. Calling it one, he says, sends one to hell as swiftly as an arrow; refusing that name does the same. He asks whether anyone in the assembly can get out of this predicament. His ensuing praise of his lineage brother at Bao'an for carrying their teacher's work forward belongs to this setting of transmission. The quotation therefore tests how to speak of an actual teacher's many teachings without settling into either verbal alternative. The immediate source introduces it simply as scripture; it does not name an individual speaker for the quoted clause. Senses.Note: Neither passage supplies a hidden identity for sandals or eggplants; the observable pair does not license a horticultural or psychological doctrine.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂：魯祖三昧最省力，纔見僧來便面壁。育王三昧又省力，纔見僧來便合掌。南山北山，如牛拽磨。脚瘦草鞋寬，地肥茄子大。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1411.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Hengchuan Xinggong. Hengchuan Rugong says, ‘Luzu’s complete command is most labor-saving: whenever he sees a monk coming, he faces the wall. Yuwang’s complete command is also labor-saving: whenever he sees a monk coming, he joins his palms. South mountain, north mountain, like an ox pulling a mill. When feet are thin, straw sandals are loose; when the soil is fertile, eggplants are large.’ Yuwang is Hengchuan’s present seat. The final pair follows a comparison of two different ways of receiving a monk; it states ordinary relations between the size of a foot and a sandal, and the quality of soil and a crop, without assigning a hidden identity to either object.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上堂。欲言言不及，林下好商量。且商量箇什麼？脚瘦草鞋寬，地肥茄子大。嫂嫂阿哥妻，師姑女人做。下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X71/X71n1422.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Nanshi Wenxiu. Nanshi Wenxiu says, ‘When you want to say it, words do not reach it; in the woods it is good to discuss. And what is there to discuss? When feet are thin, straw sandals are loose; when the soil is fertile, eggplants are large. A sister-in-law is an elder brother’s wife; a nun is a woman.’ He then leaves the seat. The saying is his answer to his own question, alongside two further plainly worded relations; it is not an unexplained quotation attributed to a third speaker.

Senses.Explanation: The fit of a sandal depends on the foot, and the size of an eggplant on the soil. Masters place these ordinary comparisons after talk of receiving monks or of what can be discussed. The two clauses name ordinary, visible relations. A sandal that is roomy around a thin foot is loose; fertile ground grows large eggplants. Nanshi Wenxiu uses the pair when he asks what there is to discuss after saying that words cannot reach it. He follows it with ‘a sister-in-law is an elder brother’s wife; a nun is a woman.’ These accompanying statements keep his answer at the level of plainly named relations rather than supplying a secret meaning for sandals or eggplants. Hengchuan Rugong gives it after comparing Luzu’s facing the wall when a monk approaches with his own joining palms at Yuwang. He calls both labor-saving and compares the two mountains to an ox turning a mill. The pair closes that contrast of different responses. The passage lets the reader see what precedes the saying, but it does not explicitly equate either master with the foot, sandal, soil or crop.

Senses.Explanation: The heel is the bodily location named in threats of a blow or spike beneath it and in following at another person’s heels. These constructions select the heel or the space immediately under it; no anatomical injury is inferred when the line merely locates a threatened action there.

Yuanwu tells a lay correspondent to make it firm; Zhongfeng finds a binding thread still under it; Wuyi asks how deep the water is beneath it. Occurrences.Kwic: 如，湛然真純，是解作活計。但一念不生，放教玲瓏，纔有是非、彼我、得失，勿隨他去，乃是終日竟夜親參自家真善知識，何憂此事不辦？切須自看。示許奉議(庭圭)示許奉議此箇事，在利根上智之人一聞千悟不為難，要須脚跟牢實、諦當徹信，把得定、作得主，於一切違順境界、差別因緣打成一片，如太虗空無纖毫障隔，湛湛虗明無有轉變，雖百劫千生始終如一，方得平穩。多見聰俊明敏、根浮脚淺，便向言句上認得轉變，即以世間無可過，尚遂增
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1357.xml). Yuanwu counsels a lay correspondent to make his own footing firm.

Occurrences.Kwic: 直下不能混入靈源併歸真際。要脫他無常生死。也大難。此事須是著實到這田地。不涉第二念不見第二人方堪負荷。苟非能所脫落身心悟徹底。自餘有一等闡提漢。趂一時狂見也隨人道。無儞無我無生無死。說得也相似。殊不知脚跟下紅絲線不斷。正是益增其識妄耳。昔靈雲和尚舉眼見桃花便道。自從一見桃花後。直至如今更不疑。香嚴和尚掃地次擊竹有聲便道。一擊忘所知更不假修持。此二尊宿便是聞聲見色徹見己躬底樣子。蓋其多生積世。參扣祖意乃

Occurrences.Kwic: 三十七，通身赤骨律，不喫常住飯，砵盂兩度濕。師云：却是汝來得，要且不會老僧意在。上堂，僧問：蟄戶將開，海門雷震，敢問和尚：一池鱣鮪，何時際會風雲？師云：拄杖時常頭點空。進云：興波作浪時如何？師云：闍黎脚跟下水深多少？僧咦云：透網金鱗雖振𩮻，冲霄丹鳳不遺苞。師云：更須桉下雲頭始得。又僧問：乍入叢林，蒙師命往白下請有字經，敢問和尚：無字經命向甚麼處請？師云：磕破髑髏。僧禮拜，師云：便祇如此耶？出去。又僧問
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1435.xml). Wuyi challenges a monk who claims to raise waves to measure water under his own heels.

Senses.Explanation: Here the heel locates a person's actual footing in the present encounter. Yuanwu uses it for settled confidence in his own letter, while Zhongfeng exposes a remaining tie beneath a claimant's talk. Wuyi asks a monk to measure the water beneath his heels rather than merely boast of raising waves. Muchen calls for standing still as the court gate opens; Tiantai Deshao urges breaking through from one's own heels. Yuanwu's portrait verse gives a different image of severing the heel. The source turns support a practical footing metaphor without making every occurrence a bodily movement.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the great matter beneath one’s heels
Senses.Note: The four cited works distinguish a quoted memorial, Yuanwu Keqin’s narration and direct address, and Ying’an Tanhua’s instruction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 適來知縣學士疏中有言：馬師圓相，遠緘千里之清規；欽老機鋒，點破一時之群惑。群惑既破，則人人脚跟下大事洞明；大事既明，則十二時中折旋俯仰、彈指謦欬，無非佛之妙用；既是佛之妙用，則不從人得；既不從人得，亦不在己躳；既不在己躳，則內不放出、外不放入；既外不放入，則外息諸緣；內不放出，則內心無喘；

Occurrences.Kwic: 巴陵眾中謂之鑒多口。常縫坐具行脚。深得他雲門脚跟下大事。所以奇特。後出世法嗣雲門。先住岳州巴陵。更不作法嗣書。只將三轉語上雲門。如何是道。明眼人落井。如何是吹毛劍。珊瑚枝枝撐著月。如何是提婆宗。銀椀裏盛雪。雲門云。他日老僧忌辰只舉此三轉語。報恩
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2003.xml). Blue Cliff Record by Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. Yuanwu Keqin narrates that Baling deeply grasped Yunmen’s great matter beneath the heels before listing Baling’s three turning words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師云。當軒正坐覿面無私。離相絕名當機有準。露箇形相通一線道。起箇面目示少津梁。如隔山見煙早知是火。隔牆見角早知是牛。若要只管隨數逐名求玄覓妙。則喪却自己脚跟下大事。埋沒從上來佛祖家風。只如今不依倚一物。不顯箇消息。還有共相證據底麼。若證據得。把斷要津不通凡聖。不向二千年前釋迦老子起模畫樣處。各自點胸。何故大丈夫兒。他人住處我不住。他人用處我不用。祖師
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. Yuanwu Keqin directly warns his audience that pursuing names and seeking marvels loses their own great matter beneath the heels.

Occurrences.Kwic: 大凡參學，末上既非正因，至竟祇成廢人。設若親近宗師，亦是沽名譽利，其脚跟下大事無因分曉。大事既不分曉，則惡業因緣從而和之。是以智者改過而遷善，愚者耻過而遂非。遷善則其德日新，遂非則其惡彌積，聖賢之語昭著明矣。儻不諄諄奉守所誡，則人天二路泯絕，驢胎馬腹無疑。豈不見汾陽云
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1359.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Ying’an Tanhua. Ying'an Tanhua tells the fundraiser Wei that mistaken study leaves the great matter beneath his heels without means of clarification.

Senses.Explanation: The great matter beneath one’s heels is the personally situated matter said to become clear, be deeply grasped, be lost, or remain unresolved. A county magistrate-scholar’s memorial says it becomes clear; Yuanwu Keqin says Baling deeply grasped it and elsewhere warns that name-chasing loses it; Ying’an Tanhua says false study leaves it without means of clarification.

Senses.PreferredTarget: deserves thirty blows at the heels
AlternateTargets: thirty staff blows would be fitting right there
Senses.Note: The phrase is a stock sharp verdict. “At the heels” makes the judgment immediate and personal; “thirty blows” is the conventional force of the rebuke in these texts.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無，污染即不得。丫角女子髮如銀，病中勘破維摩詰。即此不污染，是諸佛之所護念。粉碎虗空撲地來，百匝千重成一片。諸昆仲，既不似一物，畢竟似箇甚麼？有眼無耳朵，六月火邊坐。任是同胞生，也須更問過。更問過是甚麼？良久，卓拄杖云：拄杖子却辯得。佛誕日，上堂。王宮未降，佛事已週，脚跟下好與三十棒；未出母胎，度人已畢，脚跟下好與三十棒；四十九年說夢，取笑旁觀，脚跟下好與三十棒；三百餘會週遮，模糊正眼，脚跟下好與三十棒；忽遇惡水潑來，即周行七步，目顧四方，自云：天上天下，唯吾獨尊。脚跟下好與三十棒。獨有雲門大師云：我當時若見，一棒打死與狗子喫却，貴圖天下太平。雲門用此惡辣手段始能竪立宗乘，若是倚牆靠壁漢又胡足道，博山三十棒略與通信。座中
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X72/X72n1435.xml). Expanded Record of Chan Master Wuyi Yuanlai. Wuyi turns familiar claims into targets of a sharp verdict.

Occurrences.Kwic: 明眼人。覷見一場敗闕。且離意想絕功勳。一句作麼生道。八臂夜叉擎鐵柱。忿怒那吒撲帝鐘。上堂。壁立萬仞處透得。鬧市裏可以橫身。鬧市裏透得。壁立萬仞處可以倒退。何也根本若真。正眼洞明。則七穿八穴。根本若不明。正眼若麋麻。則皮穿骨露。故德山入門便棒。臨濟入門便喝。睦州見僧便道現成公案。資福道隔江見剎竿便去。脚跟下好與三十棒。豈不是壁立萬仞處透得大丈夫漢。一等是踏破草鞋。何不向祖佛提不起處承當。天人著眼不及處擔荷。然後即心即佛非色非心。以一重去一重。以一句脫一句。豈不是鬧市裏透得。向箇裏直得壁立萬仞。然後似鶻提鳩。所以古人道。垂手還同萬仞崖。正偏何必在安排。然後與麼也得。不與麼也得。與麼不與麼總得。似虎靠山。忽若與麼也不得
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1997.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yuanwu Foguo. Yuanwu asks whether received examples are enough.

Occurrences.Kwic: 歷歷，露堂堂。一切智智清淨中，還具縱橫殺活底道理也無？一切智智清淨。臨危不悚人，因什麼却推倒釋迦老子？天上天下，唯我獨尊。敲敲𥕤𥕤處即且置，如何是不傷物義底句？道！道！寒時普天普地寒，熱時普天普地熱。達磨西來，祇有一則奇特因緣，未敢望你會，作麼生舉？諦聽！諦聽！知有底人觸途見性，為什麼倒退三千？脚跟下好與三十棒。行脚人各各有本道公據，指什麼處為地頭？不可更指。護身符子不問你，還我祖父契書來。劈胸與一拳。丈夫漢箇箇鼻孔撩天，因什麼張公喫酒李公醉？面南看北斗。行住坐臥四威儀中，還見毗盧遮那無見頂相麼？金屑眼中翳。以有為有，是凡夫見；以有為無，是聲聞見。禪家流見山見水時如何？紅爐一點雪。舉拳，云：微塵諸佛盡
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X69/X69n1347.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Changling Shouzhuo. Changling answers a retreating posture with the stock rebuke.

Occurrences.Kwic: 入底道理？青原白家三盞酒，喫了猶道未沾脣。上堂。云：道遠乎哉？觸事而真，善因招惡果；聖遠乎哉？體之即神，刻糞作旃檀。蔣山恁麼著語，是汝諸人還知落處麼？良久，云：不因風撼庭前樹，爭見山花入袖香？長蘆到，上堂。風行草偃，水到渠成，夙世冤家，同門出入。聞禪聞道，似鴨聽雷；見佛見祖，如風過樹。隔江見剎竿便回去，脚跟下好與三十棒，未足觀光，直須眉毛廝結，同生同死。且道五逆聞雷一句作麼生道？良久，云：上大人，丘乙己。佛生日，上堂云：鐵壁，鐵壁，從來真實號之曰佛，常在苦海中立，風吹不入、水灑不濕、棒打不入，是故以本願力撈摝眾生不息。雲門忍俊不禁，打與狗喫，此意深密，非語默可及。四月八日是渠誕迹，露柱燒香湯已畢，大家送至龕室，泥人揩背

Occurrences.Kwic: 木藂林為輔弼。主賓互用，左右逢原。賓則始終賓，主則始終主。青蘿夤緣，直上寒松之頂。白雲淡泞，出沒太虗之中。端午，上堂。拈主丈：者一莖草等閑拈出，照見天下人心肝五臟、佛病祖病、一切魔病悉皆消滅，文殊、善財總摸索不著。卓主丈，下座。高麗真長老至，上堂：達磨不來東土，二祖不往西天，保壽不渡河，玄沙不出嶺，各人脚跟下好與三十棒拽取。占波國與新羅國鬪頟即且置，且道金剛山與水晶宮耳語箇什麼？擊拂子：一葉落，天下秋。小參小參□□□自然等編結制。無上法王有大陀羅尼門，圓而無內，方而無外，無內無外，聖凡普會。若入得此門，則百千三昧門、百千總持門、百千解脫門一時證入，二六時中、四威儀內撞倒燈籠、磕破露柱，且莫麤心好。睦州和尚道：未得

Senses.Explanation: “Thirty blows at the heels would be fitting” is a sharp verdict that a response or act has fallen short. Wuyi repeats the verdict after several claims in a birthday address on the Buddha, turning each into a fresh challenge. Yuanwu sets it beside the old example of blows and shouts, then asks why listeners stop with what predecessors did. Changling gives it as the answer when someone who should recognize things directly retreats. Ying’an says that turning back at the sight of a staff across the river would still merit the verdict. Yuejiang delivers it to everyone in a hall address built from old travel stories, then presses a new question.

Senses.Explanation: To have the feet planted on solid ground is to answer or investigate from firm, firsthand footing instead of relying on verbal display. Chan masters use the bodily image for an actual place to stand and for inquiry that does not float in borrowed explanation. Caoshan Baoji Xiong gives the phrase as the student’s place for settling life. Tianmu Mingben tells an inquirer to discard memorized sayings and investigate with feet on solid ground. Yuanwu Keqin contrasts such a person with an interlocutor left speechless by Muzhou. Dahui Zonggao uses the phrase for entering a demanding gate that uproots birth and death.

Hansong Zhicao answers questions about the principal and partial positions and their meeting, then makes a sequence of gestures with his whisk. Holding it upright, he says that what is originally nameless gives birth to heaven, earth and all things. Holding it across, he questions names; striking the incense stand, he speaks of existence and nonexistence appearing within one another without being held by words. He places the whisk on his shoulder and says that killing and reviving, illumination and activity, occur together, followed by the headword's four compressed expressions about penetrating the teaching and the way and carrying along the path. Sweeping the whisk, he refuses to establish existence or nonexistence, subject or object. He finally asks whether this is principal, partial or carrying both, warning against a fixed declaration through the royal-name taboo image. The phrase is Hansong's own present utterance accompanying the carried whisk. The address does not separately define its four technical terms, so the translation preserves their parallel movement without imposing a complete system on them.

Shuzhong Wuyun opens an address for visiting abbots and changes among attendants with the same four expressions, followed by saying that one sentence presents the whole and every occasion responds at once. He then raises the old Duofu case: asked what his one clump of bamboo is, Duofu says that one stalk and two stalks lean; when the monk does not understand, three stalks and four stalks are bent. Shuzhong compares this with a rope through a bull's nose and a bit in a horse's mouth, commending Duofu's extraordinary ability to meet the question through the teaching. He asks whether the monk's question leaves anything wanting and closes with a golden rooster crying from a jade railing, its sound reaching straight to the summit. Here the headword introduces a present handling of an old dialogue in a gathering of guests and attendants. Its force is shown in response and reception, not a four-part technical definition. The separate anthology copy preserves this same occasion and does not supply another independent use.

Senses.Explanation: The whole body is eyes is a stock Chan formula that makes the entire body the stated organ of seeing. Chan records make the whole body an organ of seeing, commonly beside whole-body hearing, speaking, or acting. Yuanwu says, 'the whole body is eyes, yet seeing does not reach it,' and extends the same construction to ears, mouth, and mind. Another discourse pairs 'the whole body is a mouth' with 'the whole body is eyes,' then assigns the former speech and the latter use. In public questioning, 'the Great Compassionate One does not extend a hand; the whole body is eyes' answers the class 'meaning and phrase both arrive.' Later case comments use the phrase as an appraisal of Yuanwu Keqin and as wording that itself still requires investigation.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Your whole body is food; your whole body is water
AlternateTargets: All of you is food, all of you is water
SearchAliases: whole body is food whole body is water
Senses.Note: Xuefeng speaks of people starving beside food and thirsting beside water; Xuansha sharpens the image to those immersed in what they cannot use. Yunmen answers, “Your whole body is food; your whole body is water.” Hongzhi reverses the lack into surfeit, Dahui challenges the suddenness of Yunmen’s word, Pu’an examines the three masters together, and Hengchuan speaks the pair anew before asking who is sated or soaked. The reply points past the picture of a separate person trying to obtain something outside himself.

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 和尚。僧問：古殿無佛時如何？曰：梵音何來？又問：不假修證，如何得成？曰：修證即不成。法眼禪師三界唯心頌。三界唯心，萬法唯識。唯識唯心，眼聲耳色。色不到耳，聲何觸眼。眼色耳聲，萬法成辦。萬法匪緣，豈觀如幻。大地山河，誰堅誰變。又華嚴六相頌。華嚴六相義，同中還有異。異若異於同，全非諸佛意。諸佛意總別，何曾有同異。男子身中入定時，女子身中不留意。不留意，絕名字，萬象明明無理事。青原問神會：從甚麼處來？會云：曹溪來。曰：將得甚麼物來？會振身而立。師曰：猶帶瓦礫在。會云：和尚莫有真金與人否？曰：設有，汝向甚麼處著？羅漢南和尚示眾云：紅霞穿碧落，白鷺點滄洲。不是寒山子，時臨古渡頭。騎駿馬，驟高樓，萬里銀河輥玉毬。別明真解脫，撥火覔浮漚。又示眾云：禪不禪，道不道，三寸舌頭胡亂掃。昨夜日輪飄桂花，今朝月窟出芝草。阿呵呵！萬兩黃金無處討。一句絕思量，諸法不相到。雪峯云：飯籮邊坐餓死人，臨河渴死漢。玄沙云：飯籮裏坐餓死漢，水裏沒頭浸渴死漢。雲門云：通身是飯，通身是水。妙喜舉了，喝云：多觜阿師，可殺忍俊不禁，通身是飯，通身是水，那裏得遮消息來？正法眼藏卷第一之下第二之上正法眼藏卷第二之上徑山大慧禪師宗杲集并著語後學黃葉庵沙門智舷校閱達磨大師安心法門云：迷時人逐法，解時法逐人。解則識攝色，迷則色攝識。但有心分別計較，自心現量者，悉皆是夢。若識心寂滅，無一動念處，是名正覺。問：云何自心現量？荅：見一切法有，有自不有，自心計作有。見一切法無，無自不無，自心計作無。乃至一切法亦如是，並是自心計作有，自心計作無。又若人造一切罪，自見己之法王，即得解脫。若從事上得解者，氣力壯。從事中見法者，即處處不失念。從文字解者，氣力弱。即事即法者，深從汝種種運為，跳踉顛蹶，悉不出法界，亦不入法界。若以法界入法界，即是癡人。凡有所施為，終不出法界心。何以故？心體是法界故。問：世間人種種學問，云何不得道？答：由見己故，不得道。己者，我也。至人逢苦不憂，遇樂不喜，由不見己故。所以不知苦樂者，由亡己故，得至虗無。己自尚亡，更有何物而不亡也？問：諸法既空，阿誰修道？答：有阿誰，須修道？若無阿誰，即不須修道。阿誰者，亦我也。若無我者，逢物不生是非。是者，我自是而物非是也。非者，我自非而物非非也。即心無心，是為通達佛道。即物

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 養何在？雲居云：始得孝養。自爾洞山許之，為室中領袖。拈云：一法界中，唯有洞山觀見作大五逆人是孝順子，行持孝順為大五逆人。如今普菴將什麼為孝養？瞪目四顧，良久，云：在在處處不識佛父母。又問：如何行五逆？答：羊羹細酒、齋餅饅頭，騎馬底騎馬、牽牛底牽牛，也有橫吹孤笛、也有拍掌鳴謳，唯獨一般不可說，雪人火裏趙楊州。大秤秤不起，小斗量不盡，無量劫即今，無不是心印。舉：夾山為渡子時，有一婆子抱一孩兒上船，云：呈橈舞棹都不問，且道婆子手中孩兒甚處得來？夾山以橈子便打，婆子云：婆婆有六箇孩兒，五箇不遇善知識，只這箇也不消得。遂拋向江中，夾山乃吐舌。拈云：諸方道：夾山與麼時，打著這婆婆。普菴見這婆子與夾山共一足、共隻眼、一箇口，說又說不得、去又不得、見又見不得，孩兒則不問，作麼生分別夾山吐舌之處？船子寥寥載不空，幾回明月弄清風。呈橈舞棹無佗事，只欲教人解六通。舉雪峰云：飯籬邊坐餓死人，臨河渴死漢。玄沙云：飯籬裏坐餓死漢，水裏沒頭浸渴死漢。雲門云：通身是飯，通身是水。拈云：大小大雪峰，及乎到這裏，未免破一作二。普菴念呪曰：婆嚧吃嚀，拈却飯籠邊死人。婆訶這一粒玄沙，無端被雪老引入飯裏水裏。如今大地生靈，飲水喫飯，且子細照顧。雖是玄沙，也能殺人，也能活人。祇有雲門老漢，吞聲忍氣，不能管得，所以和泥合水。何處無雲不是門，藏鋒不露理難論。雪峰未盡玄沙意，惹得村人村又村。舉：教云：城東老母與佛同時而生，一世共處，而不欲見佛。每見佛來，即便回避，周回上下皆避不得，乃以手掩面，十指掌中悉皆見佛。拈云：咄！這老婆子也是沒量己德，與佛同時，不二不生。既是取捨不得，便好堂中穩坐，飯來開口、箸來伸手，無端作得許多揑怪，教壞人家男女。若當時教普菴一見婆子，連佛一時埋却，只存箇弄影漢，時時與人方便行住坐臥，豈不快哉？又云：如今亦不欠少。似水煎茶待故人，知音喫了笑忻忻。茶水本來無一說，揚眉早是自瞞心。舉：永嘉大師云：無相無空無不空，即是如來真實相。拈云：子細思量，永嘉大師恁麼說話都無頭腦，如今一念棄捨塵緣，到處參尋知識，楖𣗖橫肩盡是學佛知見，究生死一段大事作麼生？相也無，空也無，不空又無，却教學人向什麼處摸索？○咦！不可說，不可說中又不可說，究竟如是。拈古談今我尚無，木奴艸女辨工夫，艸木恰知非外物，含靈那信自毗盧

ClaimAnchors.Kwic: 夏秋冬是物不遷義，生死去來是諸人不遷義。黃河因甚向北流？為純維那下火，一攧便扶不起。平生所做純熟底工夫，打失無留。十尊古佛，即今在火𦦨上與你說法，好生聽取。為智掌財下火，髑髏打破，智慧泯絕，三十六莖筭子撒在火裏，燒作堆灰去也。為行者下火，不著佛求，不著法求，不著僧求，十方薄伽梵，一路涅槃門。顧左右云：夜來何處火，燒出古人墳？佛涅槃，上堂。日暖風和二月春，桃紅李白遍山林，涅槃路上絕來往，一箇無為清淨身。東臯友山和尚至，上堂：發古佛心，行菩薩行。建梵剎於十字街頭，南來者休去歇去，北來者休去歇去。三十年後，破草鞋向甚處著？為默維那下火，打破生死關，見徹動靜語默本源，即是桶篐𪹼底時節。雖然，學道如鑽火，逢煙未肯休，直待金星現，燒脚又燒頭。元正，上堂：一塵入正受，諸塵三昧起。元正啟祚，萬物咸新。東海鯉魚打一棒，雨似盆傾。為聖僧侍者下火。汝名仁洽，仁德無形，沾洽萬有，汝還知麼？丹霞為甚騎聖僧？汝道得麼？石火電光休擬議，坐斷毗盧法報化。上堂：通身是飯，通身是水，浸殺底有甚數？飽殺底有甚數？拈拄杖云：歸堂去。上堂，僧問：不作佛見，不作眾生見，還得否？師云：二鐵圍山萬仞高。乃云：直下無一絲毫頭，遍界全彰奇特事。山花開似錦，㵎水湛如藍。傅大士騎牛，入你眼睛鼻孔裏去。結夏，小參。安居法門說了也，只要奉行舉足下足，自然不傷物命。護生須是殺，殺盡始安居，這箇法門亦不可不奉行。鐵船浮水上，久已傳諸方，今日青海頭，木船浮水面。為行者下火：你不知生處死處？是心未了，鬚髮不曾得；除是身未了，我一把火都與你了却。祖師道：了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別？元宵，清凉西堂至，請新知事上堂。然燈佛與清凉山萬菩薩共說無生法忍，育王寺新請職事，箇箇是了事底人。舉手云：蘇嚕蘇嚕。上堂。薪火相交，識性不停。上至諸佛，下至眾生。拈拄杖云：扶過斷橋水，伴歸明月村。解夏，小參。世尊慈悲，故出現於世，立長期、短期。今夏是短期，九十日已過，八十九日尚有一日在。你諸人有所證、無所證，不可辜負世尊、不可辜負自己。自己非泡幻者是，亦非昭昭靈靈者是。南天台、北五臺，走得遍，還自知。開爐，上堂：三世如來說妙義，炎炎火𦦨雪火飛。面前總是聽法底，識取當頭底是誰？冬夜，小參。國無定亂之劒，四海晏清，諸人脚跟下蕩蕩地，更無一塊泥𡋯礙著。你歸堂去
